title: Feed Milling process control, hygienising and compacting technology and operations

lessons.title: Process control in a modern feed mill
lessons.html:
From manual to automated control

Most larger South African mills use a PLC (programmable logic controller) and SCADA system to control routes, batching, mixing, conditioning and pelleting. The operator selects recipes and routes; the system sequences motors, opens gates, weighs ingredients and logs data. Smaller mills may still rely on manual panels and paper batch sheets. Either way, the principles of process control are the same.

Elements of control

  • Set points – target values such as conditioning temperature, steam pressure, mixer time, die speed and feeder rate.
  • Measurement – sensors for temperature, pressure, motor load (amps), level, flow and weight.
  • Control loops – the controller compares the measurement with the set point and adjusts, for example a steam valve opens more if conditioning temperature falls below set point.
  • Interlocks – prevent unsafe or wrong operation, e.g. a conveyor cannot start if the one after it is stopped, or a press cannot run if the door is open.
  • Alarms – warn of high levels, motor overload, high bearing temperature or blocked chutes.

Statistical process control

Control charts of key variables (pellet durability, moisture, batch weights) show whether the process is stable. Points outside control limits or trends in one direction signal a special cause that must be investigated before product goes out of specification.

Data and traceability

The control system records every batch: recipe, ingredient lots and weights, times, temperatures and destination bin. This record is essential for traceability, for investigating complaints and for proving that critical control points such as heat treatment were met. Manual overrides must be authorised and logged.

The manager's role

The process manager sets and approves set points with the nutritionist and quality team, makes sure instruments are calibrated, reviews alarm and override logs, and trains operators to understand why a set point exists, not just what it is.

lessons.title: Hygienising feed
lessons.html:
Why hygienise?

Raw materials, especially oilseed meals, animal proteins and grains, can carry Salmonella and other pathogens. Salmonella in poultry feed can infect flocks and enter the human food chain through eggs and meat. Hygienising is a heat (and sometimes chemical) treatment designed to reduce pathogens to safe levels.

Methods

MethodHow it works
Steam conditioningSteam heats and moistens mash before the pellet press
Hygieniser / retention conditionerHolds hot mash at temperature for a set retention time
ExpanderHigh shear, pressure and temperature for a short time
ExtrusionCooking under pressure, typical in pet food and aqua feeds
Chemical treatmentOrganic acids or formaldehyde-based products where registered

Effectiveness depends on temperature and time together, and on moisture. The validated time-temperature combination set by the quality system must be monitored at the critical control point and recorded. Product below the critical limit must be diverted or held, not sent to customers.

Avoiding recontamination

Heat treatment is wasted if the feed is recontaminated afterwards. Separate "dirty" (raw) and "clean" (post-heat) zones, cool with filtered air, prevent condensation in coolers and bins, control birds and rodents, clean coolers and conveyors after heat treatment, and take environmental swabs as scheduled.

Quality trade-offs

High temperatures can damage heat-sensitive vitamins, enzymes and amino acids such as lysine. Nutritionists may add heat-stable forms or apply enzymes after pelleting by post-pellet liquid application. The process manager must balance feed safety, nutrition and throughput.

Validation of a hygienising step is done with the quality team, for example by testing feed before and after treatment under normal running conditions. Once validated, the settings may not be changed without a documented management-of-change review.

lessons.title: Compacting: pelleting and related processes
lessons.html:
Why compact feed?

Compacting (pelleting, crumbling, cubing) presses mash into dense particles. Benefits include less selective feeding, less dust and waste, higher bulk density for transport, better feed intake and conversion in poultry and pigs, and the hygienising effect of conditioning.

The pelleting line

  1. Feeder screw controls the mash rate.
  2. Conditioner adds steam to raise temperature and moisture, activating starch and binders.
  3. Pellet press – rollers force mash through holes in a ring die; knives cut pellets to length.
  4. Cooler – counterflow air cools and dries pellets to near ambient temperature and safe moisture.
  5. Crumbler – for young birds, rollers crack pellets into crumbles.
  6. Screener – removes fines that are returned for re-pelleting.

Factors affecting pellet quality

  • Formulation – fat, fibre, protein and starch levels, and binders.
  • Particle size – finer grind usually improves durability.
  • Conditioning – steam quality (dry, saturated), temperature and retention time.
  • Die specification – hole diameter and effective thickness (compression ratio).
  • Die and roller condition and roller gap.
  • Cooling – under-cooled pellets sweat and grow mould; over-dried pellets break.

Pellet durability index (PDI) and percentage fines are measured routinely. Throughput, motor load and kWh per tonne are monitored for efficiency.

Safety on the pelleting line

Pellet presses and conditioners involve steam, hot surfaces, high torque and heavy dies. Lock out and release steam pressure before opening doors; use lifting equipment for die changes; never put hands near rollers while the die can rotate. Boilers and steam systems must be operated and inspected under the pressure equipment rules.

Key points

  • PLC/SCADA control uses set points, measurements, control loops, interlocks and alarms.
  • Batch records support traceability and prove critical limits were met.
  • Hygienising depends on temperature, time and moisture; prevent recontamination afterwards.
  • Pellet quality depends on formulation, grind, conditioning, die and cooling.
  • Lock out and release steam before working on presses and conditioners.
